title: Adding Javascript to Websites
summary: Shows the three ways to attach JavaScript to an HTML page (inline attribute, internal script element, external file) mirroring the three CSS approaches, and why script placement matters: scripts that touch elements should come after those elements, ideally just before the closing body tag.

concepts.heading: Setup
points: New project folder (named DOM) with index.html containing boilerplate, a title, a link to a blank styles.css and a single h1 reading Hello.
Until now JavaScript ran in the browser console; this lesson wires it into a real page.
The three-way split matches the CSS lessons: inline, internal, external.

concepts.heading: 1. Inline JavaScript
points: Put code in an event-handler attribute on a tag, e.g. onload on the body element. The code inside the quotes runs when the body has loaded.

Quoting trap: the attribute value is already in double quotes, so any string inside must use single quotes (alert('Hello')); otherwise the browser ends the attribute early. Editor colouring shows which parts it reads as a string.
End the statement with a semicolon.
Drawbacks, same as inline CSS: not modular, hard to debug, poor practice. Avoid it.

concepts.heading: 2. Internal JavaScript
points: Use a script element and write code between its tags. No attribute-level quoting is needed, so normal double-quoted strings work.
The browser reads the page top to bottom; on reaching the script element it runs the code immediately.
The lecture also writes type="javascript"-style attribute; (Extra) the type attribute is unnecessary in modern HTML, JavaScript is the default.

concepts.heading: 3. External JavaScript
points: Create a .js file (index.js) and reference it with a script element using the src attribute pointing at the path; the element has no content of its own.
The page then holds no JavaScript, yet behaves identically. This is the preferred approach, like external CSS.

concepts.heading: Where to put the script element
points: CSS: put the link in the head so styles load before content; at the bottom, the browser first paints an unstyled h1, then restyles it later (shown by pausing on an alert).
JavaScript is the opposite: code that looks up and changes elements fails if the elements do not exist yet.
Demo: index.js selects the h1 with document.querySelector('h1') and sets innerHTML to a new string (Good Bye). With the script after the h1, this works.
The same script in the head runs before the h1 exists; the selector returns null and the console reports it cannot set innerHTML of null.

Best practice: place the script just before the closing body tag. Extra benefit: the visible content renders first, so the page feels faster than if the browser stalls on heavy JavaScript in the head.
(Extra) Alternatives: defer attribute on a head script, or a DOMContentLoaded listener, also wait for the DOM.
